strengths: Clear problem motivation addressing genuine limitations of existing RAG approaches for secure code generation
Novel application of program slicing to extract security-focused code examples, achieving 81.5% code reduction
Comprehensive evaluation across four benchmarks, six diverse LLMs, and five baselines with extensive ablation studies
Introduction of SecurePass@k metric that jointly evaluates security and functional correctness
Consistent empirical improvements (4.8% average SecurePass@1 gain) while maintaining 98.7% of original functional correctness
Well-written paper with thorough appendices enabling reproducibility; good experimental design practices
Thorough ablation studies (Tables 2-3) validating contributions of individual components
Analysis demonstrating improvements are pipeline-driven rather than dependent on GPT-4o
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines straightforward applications of existing techniques (hierarchical summarization, program slicing, modified RRF) without significant algorithmic innovation
Unjustified hyperparameter choices: multiple thresholds (4.0, 0.75, 0.65) and 2-hop slicing limit lack justification or sensitivity analysis
Small knowledge base with only 704 vulnerabilities (372 Python, 332 C/C++), potentially limiting generalization despite showing unseen CWE type coverage
Modest improvements (4.8%) with variance across models and no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals reported
Small security benchmark: CodeGuard+ contains only 94 test cases; evaluation on functional correctness benchmarks doesn't strongly validate security-functionality trade-offs
No analysis of retrieval recall—what happens when correct CWE type ranks beyond top-k? CWE-level retrieval robustness unexplored
Using draft (potentially vulnerable) code to retrieve secure examples counterintuitive; code similarity facet often weakest in ablations (Table 3) yet still included
Modified RRF thresholding appears ad-hoc; missing comparisons with simpler alternatives (joint scoring) or other fusion methods
Missing failure analysis: no examples of failure cases, which vulnerability types benefit most, or false positives in security evaluation
Significant computational overhead (3-5 seconds per problem, 10-12% of total time); mitigation strategies mentioned but not implemented
Reproducibility concerns: GPT-4o (proprietary, closed-source) used for knowledge base construction
Some baselines evaluated on limited model sets (SafeCoder, CoSec) due to implementation constraints; INDICT shows catastrophically poor Pass@1 rates (19.8%), questioning competitiveness
Program slicing algorithm assumes accurate PDG construction; no analysis of handling parse errors or complex code structures; 2-hop limit appears arbitrary

strengths: Addresses a real and well-motivated problem with clear limitations of existing RAG approaches for secure code generation
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 6 diverse LLMs and 4 benchmarks with appropriate sampling (100 samples per problem for randomness reduction)
Proposes SecurePass@k metric that addresses a genuine limitation of SecureRate by jointly evaluating functional correctness and security
Thorough ablation studies (Sections 3.3-3.5) validate contributions of each component including knowledge base construction and hierarchical retrieval
Technical approach is sound: using PDGs for security-focused program slicing and hierarchical multi-faceted retrieval are reasonable design choices
Demonstrates consistent improvements across multiple model families and provides generalization analysis (CWE distribution coverage)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: combines well-established techniques (cluster-then-summarize, program slicing, RRF fusion) without fundamental innovation; contribution is primarily engineering-focused

Modest improvements: 4.8% absolute gain on SecurePass@1 is respectable but incremental; large variance across models (2.5-5.1%); marginal or negative gains on general code generation benchmarks (HumanEval+, BigCodeBench, LiveCodeBench) raise questions about broad applicability

Knowledge base limitations: small dataset (704 vulnerabilities, imbalanced with 372 Python/332 C/C++); no validation of GPT-4o-generated security guidelines for correctness or hallucinations; arbitrary 2-hop slicing limit lacks justification

Unjustified hyperparameters: multiple thresholds (τ_API=4.0, τ_VA=0.75, τ_Code=0.65, α=60, k=4) introduced without sensitivity analysis, justification, or ablation; rank filtering to top-10 unexplained

Evaluation methodological concerns: CodeQL has limited vulnerability detection capabilities; only 2 programming languages tested; different subsets of baselines evaluated on different models (SafeCoder, CoSec, INDICT); no statistical significance testing despite small benchmark (94 CodeGuard+ problems)

Moderate generalization: only 65% of benchmark CWE types are unseen during training (15 of 23 for Python); limited to CVE/GitHub sources; small knowledge base relative to real-world security knowledge
Computational overhead dismissed but substantial: 2.8-3.5s per sample for draft generation and vulnerability cause analysis (Table 7); significant practical limitation for deployment

Missing critical analysis: no failure case analysis, no examination of incorrect security guidelines, no qualitative evaluation of generated code examples, no inter-annotator agreement on guideline quality
Statistical rigor issues: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; single random seed per setting; results may be high-variance given benchmark size
Retrieval method appears ad-hoc: modified RRF with hard thresholding and rank filtering lacks clear motivation; unclear how thresholds were determined or tuned

strengths: Clear problem identification with concrete motivations (noise in raw security documents, overlooking security semantics in task descriptions)
Novel combination of LLM-based summarization and static program slicing for knowledge base construction, with strong empirical validation (81.5% code reduction)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 benchmarks, 6 diverse LLMs, and 5 baselines with consistent 4.8% improvement in SecurePass@1
Introduces SecurePass@k metric addressing genuine gap in evaluation (balancing security and functionality)
Thorough ablation studies systematically validating each component (knowledge base construction, all 7 retrieval facet combinations, hierarchical design)
Strong reproducibility with detailed prompts, algorithms, and demonstration that gains don't depend on GPT-4o (Table 4)
Maintains functional correctness (98.7% of original model capability) while improving security
Well-structured paper with clear presentation, good illustrative examples, and comprehensive appendices
weaknesses: Modest improvements (4.8%) combined with significant computational overhead (2.8-12.8s draft generation + 1.4-4.3s vulnerability analysis) lacks cost-benefit analysis for practical deployment
Critical design choices lack justification: modified RRF thresholding necessity not explained, hyperparameters (τ values, k=4, 2-hop limit) appear hand-tuned with no sensitivity analysis
Limited scope: evaluation restricted to Python and C/C++ only; no evaluation on JavaScript, Java, or Rust despite their importance for LLM code generation
Incomplete experimental rigor: no statistical significance testing despite LLM variance, no human evaluation of security, no failure case analysis, no retriever quality assessment
Program slicing limitations underdiscussed: 2-hop limit and its impact on multi-function vulnerabilities not analyzed, information loss not quantified
Small knowledge base (704 total vulnerabilities) raises questions about diversity and coverage; only 22 CWE types in training data
Baseline comparisons compromised by implementation constraints: SafeCoder and CoSec evaluated on only 3-4 of 6 models
Missing critical analyses: no adversarial robustness discussion, no prompt sensitivity ablation, no investigation of when retrieved guidelines might mislead models

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear identification of limitations in existing RAG approaches for secure code generation
Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation across 4 benchmarks, 6 LLMs, and 5 baselines with extensive ablation studies
Useful contribution of SecurePass@k metric that balances security and functionality, addressing real gap in evaluation
Thoughtful system design combining LLM summarization with program slicing in hierarchical knowledge base
Strong and consistent empirical results (4.8% improvement) while maintaining 98.7% functional correctness
Excellent reproducibility with detailed prompts, algorithms, and promised code release
Thorough generalizability analysis including seen/unseen CWE types, cross-language evaluation, and dynamic testing (CWEval)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—primarily an engineering contribution combining well-established techniques (summarization, slicing, RRF) without significant methodological advances
Major generalization concerns: only 3.9% improvement on unseen CWE types vs. 9-10% on seen types (2.5x drop), suggesting heavy reliance on memorization rather than generalizable principles
Small knowledge base (704 vulnerabilities, 21 CWE types) with unclear scaling properties; evaluation benchmark contains significantly more CWE types (22-23) than training
Heavy reliance on static security analysis (CodeQL) with known limitations; SecurePass@k lacks severity/exploitability distinction; no human validation of security guidelines
Significant inference overhead (5-10+ seconds per query) from multiple LLM calls with parallelization suggested but not evaluated
Arbitrary design choices with limited justification: 2-hop slicing limit, top-k=4, threshold values (4.0, 0.75, 0.65), temperature=0.2 set without ablations
Vulnerability cause analysis lacks validation—no verification that LLM-generated causes are accurate or comparison to human annotations
Program slicing analysis overclaims: 81.5% line reduction may remove contextually important code, not just irrelevant logic; no comparison to alternative slicing methods
Incomplete baseline comparisons: SafeCoder missing results on larger models, CoSec limited by tokenizer availability, INDICT uses different security tool (semgrep vs CodeQL)
Limited failure analysis with unexplained performance drops (e.g., Llama3.1-8B showing -1.0% on seen CWE types)
